html:
The Aboriginal people of Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia, shown on the map from 2000 BCE to 1715. Their ancestors walked there more than 35,000 years ago, when low seas joined it to the mainland. When the sea rose at the end of the last Ice Age and flooded Bass Strait, about 10,000 years ago, they were cut off. They lived apart from all other people for longer than almost any human group.

They formed about nine nations. They hunted wallabies and seals, collected shellfish and birds' eggs, and gathered plants, moving with the seasons. They used fire to keep open grassland, built huts and made canoes from bark. Archaeologists have long argued over why their toolkit was smaller than on the mainland, and why they seem to have stopped eating scale fish about 3,500 years ago.

The Dutch sailor Abel Tasman sighted the island in 1642. British settlers arrived in 1803, and within thirty years most of the people were dead from violence and disease. In the Black War of the 1820s and early 1830s settlers and soldiers fought them for the land. The survivors were moved to Flinders Island. Truganini, who died in 1876, was long called the last Tasmanian, but that is wrong: descendants of women taken by sealers to the Bass Strait islands survive today. Their wider story belongs with the mainland peoples in Aboriginal Australian hunter-gatherers.
